sentences.text: The name Stellasaurus translates to 'star lizard,' a reference to the unique star-like pattern of its head decorations and the famous David Bowie song 'Starman'.
This ceratopsian dinosaur featured complex cranial ornamentation, including a nasal horn that was notably larger than those found in the genus Centrosaurus.
The nasal horn stood upright, curved inward, and was flattened on its sides.
The back of the skull displayed long, straight third and fourth spines, while the fifth through seventh spines remained short and unelongated.
No separate frill ossifications (epiparietals or episquamosals) have been found in Stellasaurus, suggesting that Stellasaurus and related genera may have lacked them.
This scientific reassessment officially named it a distinct species within a newly created genus.
The describers view it as a transitional form between Styracosaurus albertensis and Einiosaurus on a lineage leading to Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
Stellasaurus belongs to the family Ceratopsidae, the class Ornithischia, and the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
The only known species is Stellasaurus ancellae, which serves as the type species for the genus.
The animal lived approximately 75 million years ago during the Campanian stage, a time window estimated between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
Contemporary dinosaurs in its environment included hadrosaurids, ankylosaurs, the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus, and smaller theropods.
Researchers differ in their interpretation of the fossil, specifically regarding the position of the neck shield and parietal spines.
There is a debate regarding the count of epiparietalia, with Andrew McDonald identifying P8 and Wilson et al. identifying P7.
Wilson et al. do not consider separate skin ossifications, or osteoderms, to have been demonstrated in Styracosaurus, Stellasaurus, and Einiosaurus.
